title: Prayer for Christian unity (18–25 January)
hook: a week when churches pray for each other

segments.voice: Yesterday, Theophany: a cross thrown into cold water, and swimmers diving after it. Your line was the waters blessed. Which water did you notice? Day one thousand seventeen.

On a weeknight in January, a Lutheran pastor reads a prayer out loud, and the name in it belongs to the Catholic parish two streets over. Across town, an Orthodox priest asks God's blessing on a Pentecostal church that meets in a former shop. A Methodist choir sings in a Baptist chapel, and nobody tries to sign anybody up. For one week, churches that disagree about baptism, bishops and bread stop to pray for each other by name. Not to settle the arguments. Just to pray. Behind that week sits a single night, a table, and a prayer Jesus prays for people who will come after his friends. Today, the Prayer for Christian unity.
screen: `A PRAYER WITH ANOTHER CHURCH'S NAME IN IT.`

segments.voice: John's Gospel slows right down on the night before Jesus dies. After the supper, after the long talk with his friends, he looks up and prays, and the whole of chapter seventeen is that prayer. Partway through, he turns from the friends in the room to everyone who will come after them. In the King James Bible: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me." Notice what kind of sentence that is. It isn't a rule. Nobody is ordered to be one. It's a request, made to God, about the friends. Unity here is something Jesus asks for, not something he hands out as homework. And notice the pattern it points to: one the way the Father and the Son are one. Not identical. Not merged into a single shape. Close, and turned toward each other. That's why the week takes the form it does. Churches don't use it to pretend their differences are gone. Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants still hold different views about how the church is ordered, who presides at communion, and what unity would finally look like. Some hope for one visible church. Some think unity already exists underneath the different names. The week doesn't decide between them. It asks each church to pray the prayer Jesus prayed, and to say the other church's name while doing it. Look at the last clause too: that the world may believe. In the prayer, how Christians treat each other is part of how anyone else hears the message at all. A family that only argues is hard to listen to.

Here's the practice: bring to mind a church you've never set foot in. Maybe the one with the unfamiliar name on the corner. A chapel you pass on the bus. A congregation that worships in a language you don't speak. Settle, and breathe. Picture the door, the people going in, someone setting out chairs. If you pray, you can hold that church before God by name, and ask good things for it. If you don't, simply wish it well, the people inside and the work they do. Stay with that one place, the door, the chairs, the people. The bell holds the time.
Hen. Greek for one, the word in Jesus's prayer that the Father and the Son, and all who follow, may be one.
Your line: that they may be one. Today, say one kind, true thing about a church that isn't yours, out loud, to someone. Day one thousand seventeen.

howItsDone: During the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, churches of different traditions hold shared services, swap pulpits or choirs, and include one another by name in their prayers.

original.note: Greek: one. John 17 asks that the believers may be one, as the Father and the Son are one.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite week when churches are nice to each other.
what it means: churches that still disagree praying for one another by name, using the prayer Jesus prayed on his last night.
